Metric Trees and Driver Models

How does the North Star connect to the levers each team actually owns?

The Tuesday Before the Board Meeting

Bengaluru, the morning of October 6, 2026. Divya Konduri, head of product analytics at Kanak Bazaar, a quick-commerce grocery app promising delivery inside twenty minutes across nine Indian cities, opened her laptop three hours before the quarterly business review and found a message from the founder-CEO, Rohan Sethi: “Marketing spend up 40 percent, GMV up one percent. Explain it before the board explains it for us.”

The number at stake was concrete. Gross merchandise value had been ₹133.66 crore in August. The growth team had then raised the monthly performance-marketing budget from ₹3.2 crore to ₹4.5 crore specifically to pull in new ordering households ahead of the festive quarter, and the board had modelled September GMV at roughly ₹145 crore on the strength of that spend. The actual number, when finance closed the books on October 4, was ₹134.88 crore — essentially flat. If Divya walked into the review with fifty scattered dashboard tiles, the meeting would dissolve into a debate about whose creative was weaker. What she had instead was a metric tree: a decomposition of the North Star, monthly GMV, into the three levers that actually produced it, each one sitting on a named desk in a named city. That tree, not any single chart, was what let her tell the board exactly which lever had moved, by how much, and whose job it was to fix it.

The Idea: Turning One Number Into Its True Causes

A metric tree, also called a driver tree or KPI tree, is a hierarchical decomposition of one top-level outcome metric — the North Star — into the smaller metrics that multiply or add together to produce it exactly, continued downward through as many levels as there are teams who can independently move a lever. The decomposition is not a matter of taste: it is an identity. For Kanak Bazaar, monthly GMV equals the number of active ordering customers, times the number of orders each of them places, times the average value of an order. Multiply those three numbers and the units cancel to rupees; there is no rounding, no judgment call, no room for two people to disagree about whether the equation holds.

The technique descends from DuPont analysis, devised inside the DuPont corporation in the 1920s by the financial executive F. Donaldson Brown, who split return on equity into profit margin, asset turnover and financial leverage so that headquarters could see which of three very different management decisions was driving a subsidiary's return. Product organisations adopted the same discipline for growth roughly a decade ago, formalised publicly through funnel frameworks such as Dave McClure's 2007 “AARRR” and later through the North Star framework popularised by writers such as Sean Ellis and John Cutler around 2017–2019, which insisted that a single outcome metric be tied to a small set of input metrics each owned by a real team.

The idea solves a specific problem: a dashboard can display fifty metrics moving in fifty directions without ever forcing anyone to explain the one number the board actually cares about. A metric tree forces algebraic accountability. Divya's sentence for the boardroom, the one she could say without sounding glib, was this: “Our North Star never moves on its own; it moves because exactly one or two of a small number of levers moved, and the tree tells us which ones, and whose desk they sit on.”

How a Metric Tree Actually Gets Built

Building one is a sequence, and practitioners routinely skip the steps that feel obvious until the tree fails to reconcile. First, pick the North Star: a single metric that expresses the value the product actually delivers, not merely the value that is easiest to measure. Second, write the identity that produces it exactly, using only multiplication or addition of components that can each be measured independently — for Kanak Bazaar, active ordering customers times orders per active customer times average order value, an identity that must hold to the rupee, not approximately.

Third, assign each branch to the one team that can move it this quarter, which is a different question from who is merely affected by it. Everyone at Kanak Bazaar cares about GMV; only the growth pod in Bengaluru can add active customers, only Kabir Anand's retention and CRM pod in Gurugram can lift orders per customer, and only Meera Iyer's catalog and merchandising pod in Chennai can move average order value. Fourth, recurse one level further inside each branch until reaching a metric small enough for one team to act on inside a single week: active customers split into new, reactivated and retained; frequency is driven by app-open rate, push-notification click-through, and delivery reliability, the last of which belongs partly to Priya Nair's operations team in Pune, since a late or cancelled order visibly suppresses the customer's next one. Fifth — and this is the step most often skipped — attach to every leaf an owner's name, a reporting cadence, and the decision that metric is meant to inform; a tree of elegant boxes that nobody reviews on a fixed schedule is a slide, not a management system. Sixth, reconcile: the leaves must sum or multiply back to the parent using the same period and currency definitions, or the tree only looks rigorous.

The Arithmetic Divya Put on the Screen

Divya walked the board through the numbers line by line. In August, Kanak Bazaar had 8,40,000 active ordering customers, each placing an average of 2.6 orders that month, at an average order value of ₹612. Multiplying gives 8,40,000 × 2.6 = 21,84,000 orders, and 21,84,000 × ₹612 = ₹1,33,66,08,000, or ₹133.66 crore — the August GMV everyone in the room already knew.

September told a more interesting story. Active ordering customers had actually risen to 9,10,000, up 8.3 percent, which meant the extra marketing spend had done exactly what it was bought to do. But orders per active customer had fallen to 2.45, a drop of 5.8 percent, and average order value had softened slightly to ₹605, down 1.1 percent. Multiplying the actual September figures: 9,10,000 × 2.45 = 22,29,500 orders, and 22,29,500 × ₹605 = ₹1,34,88,47,500, or ₹134.88 crore — a 0.9 percent increase in GMV against a 40 percent increase in the spend meant to drive it.

Divya then ran a second pass, changing exactly one input to isolate the culprit. She held September's actual customer count and average order value fixed, but restored frequency to August's 2.6 orders per customer: 9,10,000 × 2.6 = 23,66,000 orders, and 23,66,000 × ₹605 = ₹1,43,14,30,000, or ₹143.14 crore — ₹8.26 crore higher than what had actually happened, and within striking distance of the ₹145 crore the board had modelled. That single substitution was the whole diagnosis: acquisition had delivered as promised, and the shortfall lived almost entirely inside Kabir's frequency branch, not Rohan's acquisition branch that the extra marketing rupees had targeted.

Seven Distinctions a Careful Analyst Must Hold Onto

A tree is not an org chart. A metric tree is a mathematical decomposition of a number; an org chart is a decomposition of authority. The two should overlap by design — every leaf should have a single owning team — but a tree built to mirror existing reporting lines rather than the true drivers of the North Star will hide levers that fall between two desks, such as delivery reliability at Kanak Bazaar, which belongs partly to operations and partly to retention.

Multiplicative and additive decomposition are not interchangeable. Active customers is an additive branch (new plus reactivated plus retained sum exactly to the total); GMV itself is a multiplicative branch (customers times frequency times value). Analysts who add where they should multiply, or who let a customer appear in both the “new” and “reactivated” leaves, produce a tree that no longer reconciles to the parent number, and nobody notices until the totals visibly disagree.

Branches are rarely independent. A discount campaign can raise orders per customer while depressing average order value in the same week, because shoppers place more, smaller, deal-chasing baskets. Reading Kabir's frequency number and Meera's AOV number as separate stories, rather than as two faces of the same customer behaviour, risks a diagnosis that credits or blames the wrong team.

The North Star is a lagging scoreboard; the leaves are the leading levers. GMV tells the board what already happened last month. The tree's entire value is that its lower leaves — push click-through rate, delivery SLA, cross-sell attach rate — can be measured and acted on this week, before the lagging number even closes.

A leaf without an owner, a cadence and a decision is decoration. A metric on a slide that nobody reviews on a fixed schedule, and that no one would change a specific decision in response to, is not being managed; it is being displayed.

The tree tells you what moved, almost never why. Divya's arithmetic proved that frequency had fallen; it could not say whether that was because a rival's faster app in Chennai had won share of orders, because a delivery-partner shortage was showing up as cancelled orders, or because a loyalty programme had quietly lapsed. Answering why requires cohort interviews, support-ticket review, and app-store feedback — qualitative work no amount of further decomposition replaces.

Clean identities exist mainly for revenue-like metrics. GMV decomposes exactly because customers, frequency and value are genuinely multiplicative. Trust-like constructs — app-store rating, Net Promoter Score, brand recall — do not decompose into an exact identity; forcing them into tree form produces a correlational driver model dressed up as an equation, and treating its coefficients as precise as Divya's arithmetic is a quiet but serious overreach.

How the Tree Changes Shape by Business and by Stage

A consumer app like Kanak Bazaar naturally decomposes into customers, frequency and value because each transaction is small, frequent, and driven largely by the same household. A B2B software business looks different: its North Star is typically net revenue retention, which splits into gross retention and expansion revenue, owned respectively by customer success and account management rather than by a marketing pod, and it moves on a quarterly renewal cadence rather than a weekly ordering one. A marketplace such as Kanak Bazaar also carries a second, parallel tree on the supply side — dark-store fulfilment capacity, rider availability, stock-out rate — that must reconcile against the demand-side tree Divya presented, since a demand lever pulled too hard without matching supply simply produces cancelled orders that erase the gain; this supply-side extension is the subject the next topic in this module takes up directly.

Company stage matters just as much as business model. In Kanak Bazaar's seed years, three people covered the entire tree between them and a two-level version was sufficient. After its Series D, with dedicated pods in four cities, the tree grew a third and fourth level inside each branch, and the discipline of assigning a single named owner to each leaf became the difference between a tool the board could trust and a diagram nobody could act on.

Where Metric Trees Go Wrong

The first failure shows up as a room full of people unable to explain a number's move in one paragraph, even with fifty dashboards open; the underlying error is metrics accumulated without decomposition, so more measurement produces more noise rather than more insight, and the fix is to ask, of any headline metric, which three sub-metrics would explain a five-percent move — if no one answers instantly, no real tree exists yet.

The second failure is two teams both claiming credit for the same uptick, which usually means a leaf metric has been assigned to more than one owner; the cheapest diagnostic is simply to list every leaf against a single name and flag any leaf with two.

The third is leaf metrics that improve quarter after quarter while the North Star stays flat, which points to a leakage term missing from the tree — cancellations, refunds, or churn happening between the gross and net version of a number; reconciling the sum of leaf contributions against the North Star's actual change will surface the unexplained residual immediately.

The fourth is a branch owner declaring victory after a short-lived spike from a promotion, mistaking a temporary pulse for a durable shift in the underlying rate; the cheapest check is to look at the same metric two weeks after the promotion ends, since a rate that reverts has not actually moved.

What the Same Tuesday Looks Like Done Well

In the version of Kanak Bazaar that got this right earlier, Kabir's Gurugram pod would have caught the frequency slide inside three weeks, not one quarter, because the retention branch was reviewed every Friday against a pre-agreed threshold: if orders per customer moved more than two percent week over week, the meeting's only agenda item became explaining why, before the drift compounded into a lagging GMV surprise. Rohan's growth spend would then have been redirected the same week the threshold tripped, rather than after a board member asked the question for him. The tree, reviewed at the cadence its leaves actually move, converts a quarterly postmortem into a weekly correction.

What Divya Decided

Divya told the board she was pausing the incremental festive-quarter marketing increase and redirecting roughly ₹1.5 crore of it toward the frequency and basket-value branches: a subscription push that Kabir's team had already designed, and a cross-sell placement redesign Meera's catalog team had ready but unfunded. She also proposed a standing weekly review, with all three branch owners and Priya's operations team present, gated on the same thresholds the “done well” version of the story used. The reasoning she gave the board was the tree itself: acquisition had already delivered what it was paid to deliver, and every further rupee spent there would buy customers who then had nowhere better to reorder.

The natural next readings are metric ownership and cadence, which formalises exactly the weekly-review discipline Divya was reaching for, and metric trees for two-sided products, which extends this same identity to the supply side a marketplace like Kanak Bazaar cannot ignore. Two questions worth sitting with: if your own team's North Star dropped two percent next month, could you name the three leaf metrics you would check first, and who owns each one? And where in your product does a lever that helps one branch of the tree quietly hurt another?

Metric Trees and Driver Models

A decomposition is cheap. A decomposition that survives contact with a concentrated customer base, a cost branch, a feedback loop and a compensation plan is the thing experts are actually arguing about.

1. Two rooms, one week apart

On the morning of 8 September 2026, Shaunak Bose, vice-president of product at Rangat Studio, a Bengaluru company whose app turns phone photographs and short clips into finished creative work using generative models, was looking at two numbers that pointed in opposite directions. Revenue for August had come in at ₹11.27 crore, up 6.8 percent on June. Contribution margin — revenue minus the inference and storage cost of actually producing the renders — had fallen from ₹7.37 crore to ₹7.00 crore, down 4.9 percent. Every leaf on the growth team's dashboard was green: subscribers up from 2,45,000 to 2,71,000, renders per subscriber up from 34 to 41, the latter a quarter's work by the engagement pod. The company's metric tree, drawn eighteen months earlier when Rangat sold a flat ₹499 subscription and ran one small model, rooted at revenue. Under that tree, August was an excellent month. Under the income statement, it was not.

Seven days later and 840 kilometres away, Malini Rau, chief product officer of Prayukti Systems in Pune, was preparing for a board offsite with a different kind of problem. Prayukti sells claims-automation software to general insurers and broking houses; its opening annual recurring revenue on 1 April 2026 was ₹148.0 crore across sixty-one accounts. Trailing twelve-month expansion of ₹22.9 crore, contraction of ₹6.1 crore and churn of ₹9.4 crore put net revenue retention at ₹155.4 crore over ₹148.0 crore, or 105.0 percent. The board wanted 118 percent, and a director had asked, reasonably enough, for "the NRR tree — the drivers, with owners". Malini had built exactly that tree and did not believe it. Her largest account carried ₹14.2 crore of ARR, 9.6 percent of the book; the top five carried ₹51.3 crore, 34.7 percent. A single renewal conversation in Mumbai could move the company's headline ratio by nine points. A tree of rates averaged over sixty-one accounts was arithmetically correct and managerially close to meaningless.

The two situations look unrelated and are in fact the same situation. Both companies have a decomposition that is algebraically perfect and decision-theoretically broken — Rangat's because it is rooted at the wrong quantity, Prayukti's because its leaves are statistics computed on a base far too small to behave like one. The distance between a competent practitioner and an expert in this topic is almost entirely the distance between building the identity and knowing these two failures when they appear.

2. The idea, and the three schools that disagree about it

A metric tree is a hierarchical decomposition of one top-level outcome metric into constituent metrics that combine, by a stated arithmetic rule, to produce it — continued downward until each terminal node is small enough that one named team can move it inside one planning cycle. A driver model is the weaker, broader object: a mapping from input quantities to an outcome in which the relationship is estimated rather than defined. The distinction matters more than any other idea on this page. In an identity node the relationship between child and parent is true by construction and says nothing about causality: subscribers × ARPU = revenue holds whether or not raising subscribers is a good idea. In a driver node it is an empirical claim with a coefficient, an interval and the possibility of being wrong: claims-volume coverage predicts renewal is a statement next year's data can falsify.

The technique's lineage runs through finance. F. Donaldson Brown's decomposition of return on equity into margin, asset turnover and leverage, built inside DuPont in the 1910s and carried into General Motors in the 1920s, established the form: one ratio, split into factors that multiply back exactly, each attached to a different managerial decision. Kaplan and Norton's balanced scorecard (1992) and the strategy maps that followed added a claim Brown never made — that the links between the boxes were causal. Jay Forrester's system dynamics, later taught by John Sterman, attacked exactly that claim: real businesses contain stocks, delays and feedback loops, and any tree is a snapshot of a system that has cycles in it. Product management inherited the form late and casually, through Dave McClure's 2007 funnel, Amazon's doctrine of controllable input metrics reviewed weekly (documented by Colin Bryar and Bill Carr in 2021), and the North Star framework popularised around 2017 to 2019 by Sean Ellis, John Cutler and the Amplitude group.

Three positions are live today and practitioners rarely notice which one they hold. The identity purists will sign "every node must reconcile to its parent to the rupee, in the same period, or it does not belong in the tree." They will not sign "put the estimated elasticity of retention on activation into the tree as a node," because an estimate that drifts turns the tree into a model nobody can audit. The driver modellers, whose lineage is econometric and whose modern descendants build marketing-mix and causal-graph models, will sign "a node earns its place only if intervening on it changes the parent," and will refuse to sign "customers × frequency × value explains the month," because an identity does not explain, it merely relabels. The coordination pragmatists — mostly operators — will sign "a slightly wrong tree that every team shares beats a correct tree nobody owns," and will not sign "wait for the causal work before publishing the tree." All three are defensible, and the rest of this page is an account of where each is right.

3. Mechanics: what experts actually do, including the steps left implicit

The first implicit step is choosing the root, and the choice is a strategy statement disguised as a measurement decision. Rangat's tree rooted at revenue because in 2024 marginal cost per user was negligible; by 2026 inference cost was 37.9 percent of revenue and the root should have moved. Write Rangat's real root as Π = S·A − S·R·c, where S is paying subscribers, A is ARPU, R is renders per subscriber and c is cost per render. For August: 2,71,000 × ₹416 = ₹11.27 crore of revenue, and 2,71,000 × 41 × ₹3.84 = ₹4.27 crore of cost, leaving ₹7.00 crore. The same arithmetic for June gives ₹10.56 crore minus ₹3.20 crore, or ₹7.37 crore.

The second implicit step is computing elasticities rather than admiring the diagram. For a purely multiplicative tree every factor has elasticity exactly one — a one percent move in any factor moves the root one percent — which is precisely why multiplicative trees are so bad at telling you where to work. The moment the root contains a subtraction the elasticities separate, and they separate a great deal. Differentiating, the elasticity of contribution with respect to ARPU is R/Π = 11.27/7.00 = 1.61; with respect to cost per render it is −C/Π = −4.27/7.00 = −0.61; with respect to renders per subscriber, identically −0.61; and with respect to subscribers it is (R−C)/Π = 1.00, because subscribers scale revenue and cost together. Shaunak's engagement pod had spent a quarter driving renders per subscriber up by 20.6 percent, which by this arithmetic subtracted roughly 12.6 percent from contribution before any offsetting retention benefit — a benefit that is real but sits in a driver node, estimated, not an identity node.

The third implicit step is attribution when more than one factor moves at once, and it is where competent practitioners quietly produce numbers that depend on the order they did the arithmetic in. Consider Padav Stays, a Mumbai homestay marketplace whose monthly room-nights equal unique searchers × search-to-booking conversion × nights per booking. In February 2026 that was 24.0 lakh × 3.10% × 2.40 = 1,78,560 room-nights; in May, 27.6 lakh × 2.86% × 2.62 = 2,06,812, a gain of 28,252. Substituting one factor at a time in the order searchers, conversion, nights attributes +26,784 to searchers; doing it in the order nights, conversion, searchers attributes +26,975 to the same factor. The clean solution is to work in logarithms, where a multiplicative identity becomes additive and the allocation is order-free: ln(1.150) + ln(0.9226) + ln(1.0917) = 0.13976 − 0.08059 + 0.08771 = 0.14688 = ln(2,06,812 / 1,78,560) exactly. Scaling each log share onto the rupee or unit change gives a single defensible answer, which for symmetric two-factor cases coincides with the Shapley value.

The fourth implicit step is getting stocks and flows right. Active users, installed base, accounts and subscribers are stocks; new, reactivated and churned are flows. A tree that decomposes a stock into a sum of flows without the closing-balance equation — St = St−1 + new + reactivated − churned — double-counts the moment a user leaves and returns inside the period, and the error is invisible because both halves still look plausible. The fifth, almost never written down, is matching each node's review cadence to its noise floor. Rangat's renders-per-subscriber series has a week-on-week standard deviation of about 1.8 percent; a weekly review with a two percent alert threshold trips on noise in roughly a quarter of all weeks, which trains the room to ignore the alarm. Reading a genuine two percent shift needs a four-week window or a lower-variance segment. The sixth is reconciliation: leaf contributions must close against the actual change in the root, and the residual must be named — cancellations, refunds, credits — rather than absorbed silently into the largest branch.

4. When the technique applies, stated as claims you can test

Five conditions can be written as falsifiable claims, and each is worth applying to both protagonists. One: the root decomposes into an identity whose components are independently measured. Rangat passes; Prayukti passes in rupee terms but not in ratio terms, since NRR is a quotient whose denominator is fixed in April and whose numerator is a handful of negotiations. Two: each leaf is computed on a base large enough to be read at the review cadence. Rangat passes on 2,71,000 subscribers; Prayukti fails decisively on sixty-one accounts, which is why Malini's distrust of her own tree is correct rather than squeamish. Three: each leaf has a team that can move it within one planning cycle without another team's consent. Rangat passes for cost per render and fails for ARPU, which needs the founder and finance to agree a price change; Prayukti fails for coverage, which depends on the customer's IT roadmap and therefore sits outside the firm altogether. Four: cross-elasticities between branches are small relative to own-elasticities. Rangat fails — renders per subscriber is simultaneously a cost driver and a retention driver, so the branches couple with opposite signs. Five: the root is what the business is optimising over the horizon at which the tree is reviewed. A company building a multi-year stock — installed base, licence, brand — that reviews a monthly flow tree is systematically misdirected by it.

Where the idea is actively misleading, rather than merely unhelpful, is a shorter list. Before product-market fit the identity is stable while the business model is not, so the tree lends spurious rigour to denominators that will not exist in six months. During a deliberate model change — Rangat moving from flat subscription to credits — the series under every leaf is broken and the tree keeps reporting, confidently, on a company that no longer exists. And when a leaf is a regulatory constraint rather than a lever, treating it as a lever is the most expensive mistake in the field, which is the Mandakini Finserv case below.

5. Hard edges: seams, sides, regulation, hardware and AI

The organisational seam is where trees actually fail. Every tree has nodes no single team owns: Rangat's cost per render is set jointly by the model the research group ships and the routing the platform group writes, while Prayukti's coverage is produced by a customer-success manager in Hyderabad, an implementation partner and the insurer's own data team. Mature companies say they solve this with a RACI matrix; mostly they name one accountable owner who does not control the node, list the others as contributors, and let the real allocation settle each quarter in the planning negotiation. That is less a failure of discipline than an acknowledgement that the tree decomposes arithmetic and the company decomposes authority, and the two are not isomorphic.

Two-sided products carry two trees joined at a node neither side owns — match rate, fill rate, liquidity — and the standard error is to give each side its own North Star, then find a quarter later that demand growth converted entirely into cancellations. Multi-product companies face a subtler version: the company tree sums products, but the customer who buys two is not two customers, so the cross-product cohort exists in the business and not in the arithmetic. Regulated products contain capped nodes — a lender under the Reserve Bank of India's digital lending framework cannot treat pricing, data collection or default-loss arrangements as free parameters — and those belong on the diagram as constraints, visually distinct from levers, so a growth plan cannot quietly route through one. Hardware-plus-software businesses must distinguish units shipped from units commissioned, because the channel holds inventory for months. AI-native products push cost per unit of value back into the root for the first time in a decade of software, which is why Rangat's predicament would have been unimaginable to a 2018 SaaS team and is now ordinary; they also add a quality node — render fidelity, answer usefulness — that has no identity above it and must be carried as an estimated driver.

6. Nine things that separate the expert from the competent

An identity explains nothing. The tell is someone saying "we need to raise AOV" or "we need to raise NRR" as though these were levers. They are outcomes of levers; the identity says where the number moved and is silent on why. Experts treat it as a search index and reach for cohorts, tickets and interviews the moment it points somewhere.

Attribution depends on arithmetic order. The tell is two analysts presenting different contribution percentages from the same table, each certain. The obvious reading — that one made an error — is usually wrong; both did valid chained substitutions in different orders. Experts work in logs, or state the ordering convention in the footnote.

Ratio nodes hide composition shifts. Average order value, ARPU and conversion can each fall while every segment rises, because the mix shifted toward a lower segment. The tell is a leaf declining with no segment declining. Simpson's paradox is not a curiosity here; it is the ordinary state of any ratio computed across a changing customer mix.

Stocks are not flows. The tell is an active-user tree whose branches are new, reactivated and retained with no churn term, or a hardware tree rooted in shipments. Experts insist on the closing-balance identity before looking at anything beneath it, because a stock decomposed without its outflow reconciles to the wrong parent indefinitely without ever looking wrong.

Cadence must clear the noise floor. The tell is a weekly review where the same leaf is "concerning" every third week and no action follows. Granularity is not free: each level down shrinks the base and raises the variance, so a four-level tree is reviewed at its leaves on samples too small to read at the frequency the calendar demands.

Elasticity is not importance until multiplied by feasibility. A multiplicative tree makes every branch look equally powerful. The expert ranks by elasticity × the move the team can credibly deliver × confidence the move is causal — which is how a 0.61-elasticity infrastructure node beat a 1.61-elasticity pricing node at Rangat.

Branches covary, often with opposite signs. The tell is the sum of branch wins exceeding the root's actual move, quarter after quarter. Discounting raises frequency and cuts basket value; engagement raises retention and cost. Experts draw the known couplings as edges, because an unwritten coupling becomes an argument between two teams who are both telling the truth.

The leaves degrade the moment they are compensated. Goodhart's law arrives at the leaf, never the root, because the root is too far from anyone's control to game. The tell is green leaves and a flat root: every terminal metric improving and the North Star unmoved for three quarters. The diagnostic is to ask what behaviour would maximise the leaf while harming the parent, then check whether anyone is doing it.

Changing the tree is a strategy change. Organisations do it either far too often, destroying the comparability of their own series, or far too rarely, running a tree built for a model they abandoned two years ago — Rangat's case exactly. The expert versions the tree with a date, keeps the old root computed in parallel for two quarters, and treats the re-root as a board item rather than analytics housekeeping.

7. How it differs by product type and by stage

Consumer transactional products decompose cleanly and multiplicatively because transactions are numerous, small and homogeneous; the honest statement is that most of the published literature is about this case and generalises worse than it admits. Subscription B2B substitutes an additive ARR ledger for a multiplicative volume identity, and its real difficulty is not the arithmetic but the account concentration described above: below roughly a hundred accounts, rates stop being statistics. Enterprise deepens this until the tree is properly an account plan with arithmetic attached. Platforms and marketplaces need the two-sided treatment and a shared liquidity node. Hardware adds a channel-inventory stock and a multi-quarter lag between the flow a team controls and the stock the root depends on, so review cadence and causal horizon come apart. AI products, uniquely among software, put a variable cost per unit of delivered value into the root and a non-identity quality node into the middle of the diagram.

Where the difference is not real is worth saying plainly. The arithmetic of decomposition, the logarithmic attribution, the stock-flow discipline and the ownership rule are identical across all of these; the claims that B2B "needs a different framework" or that AI products "cannot be decomposed" are, in the main, marketing. Stage matters in one specific way: at seed the tree should be two levels and reviewed monthly, because the leaves have no statistical power and the root is changing shape; from Series B the third level pays for itself; past Series D the binding constraint is no longer arithmetic but whether each leaf has exactly one name against it, and the commonest late-stage pathology is a handsome four-level tree in which nine leaves have two owners and four have none.

8. Three worked cases, one of them a failure

Padav Stays, above, is the clean case: three factors moving at once, a correct log attribution, and a conclusion the chained method muddies — the 0.24-point conversion decline destroyed 55 percent of what searcher growth created, so the traffic win was substantially self-cancelling and the right next investment was search relevance, not more searchers.

Mandakini Finserv, a Chennai lending app, is the failure. Its tree rooted at monthly disbursal and split into installs, application-completion rate, approval rate and ticket size, each with an owner and a weekly cadence — textbook, by the standards of section three. Over five months from June 2025 approval rose from 18.4 percent to 26.1 percent and monthly disbursal from ₹88 crore to ₹127 crore. The tree had no risk branch, because credit risk sat in a separate function with a quarterly cadence and a metric — 90-days-past-due — that does not mature for six to nine months. By March 2026, the incremental ₹184 crore of disbursal originated under the loosened policy was running at 7.8 percent lifetime credit loss against 3.4 percent underwritten, an excess of roughly ₹8.1 crore, with a further ₹2.4 crore of collections cost. Approval rate had never been a lever; it was a policy constraint owned by the credit committee, and putting it on a product tree with a weekly target converted a risk appetite into a growth dial. The recovery took two quarters: the root moved from disbursal volume to risk-adjusted contribution per rupee disbursed; first-EMI default, readable at forty-five days, was added so the risk branch could be reviewed at the volume branch's weekly cadence; and approval rate was redrawn as a constraint box with no target attached to it at all.

Parvat Instruments, a Coimbatore maker of solar inverters with a paid monitoring subscription, is the instructive middle case. Its software revenue tree read installed base × attach rate × subscription ARPU, and in FY26 the team forecast from 41,000 units shipped. Only 29,400 were commissioned inside the year; 11,600 sat in distributor warehouses, and software revenue landed roughly 39 percent below forecast without any leaf being wrong. The fix was to insert the channel as an explicit stock — shipped, held, commissioned — and to define the node as units that had sent a first telemetry heartbeat, an event the company observed directly rather than inferring from an invoice.

9. Failure modes and the questions that catch them early

Table 2 — The five failures that account for most broken trees in practice, with the question that surfaces each one before it is expensive.
FailureEarly signDiagnostic questionCost if caught late
Wrong root (tree scores the wrong objective)Leaves green, income statement redIf every leaf hit target, would the P&L improve?A full quarter of roadmap spent widening a loss
Missing branch (risk, cost or leakage)Residual between leaf sum and root change grows monthlyWhat is the unexplained residual this month, by name?Mandakini's ₹10.5 crore, discovered at maturity
Rate on a concentrated baseOne account moves the headline by pointsWhat is the top-five share of the denominator?Targets set on a number the team cannot influence
Goodharted leafLeaf improves for three quarters, root flatHow would I maximise this leaf while hurting the parent?An incentive plan that has to be unwound publicly
Cadence below the noise floorSame alert every third week, no actionWhat is this leaf's week-on-week standard deviation?Alert fatigue; the real move is missed inside the noise

Four of the five are not arithmetic errors at all — the trees reconciled perfectly throughout — but errors about what the arithmetic was for. That is why review discipline catches them and better dashboards do not.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Identities versus estimated drivers. The purist case: an identity can be audited by anyone, cannot drift, and survives turnover; admit estimated coefficients and you have a model whose maintenance nobody owns and whose errors compound silently. The modeller's case: an identity has zero decision content — it says where the number moved, never which intervention would move it — and a tree of identities flatters whichever team happened to own the branch that moved. The purist is wrong if estimated nodes can be re-fitted on a fixed cadence with published intervals; the modeller is wrong if those re-fits do not happen and the coefficients rot.

Trees versus loops. The system-dynamics objection is that a tree cannot represent retention feeding referral feeding acquisition, and that every business of consequence contains such a loop, so the tree is a lie that gets more misleading the better the business is working. The operator's reply is that a loop model no one can read produces no decisions, and that a tree with two or three known loops annotated captures most of the value at a tenth of the cost. The operator is wrong when loop gain is high and delays long — marketplaces near a liquidity threshold, products with strong word-of-mouth — where the tree under-attributes the compounding branch.

Should the tree carry accountability at all? The coordination case is that a metric without an owner is decoration and ownership is the entire point. The opposing case, held by those who have watched Goodhart arrive on schedule, is that the tree should be an instrument of diagnosis and never of compensation, because the moment a leaf becomes a bonus the leaf-to-root relationship decays. The evidence on both sides is anecdotal, which is itself a finding: this is the largest open question in the topic and the field has no controlled evidence on it.

One root or several? Single-root advocates point to the coordination benefit of one number. The multi-root position — closer to the balanced scorecard, and to how Rangat should have been set up — holds that any real business optimises a constrained objective, growth subject to margin and quality, and that collapsing it hides which constraint binds. What would settle it is evidence that single-root organisations recover faster from constraint violations; nobody has it.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this builds the tree, assigns owners and publishes it. Someone who has internalised it starts from the decision the tree is meant to inform and refuses any node that changes no decision. They compute elasticities before choosing a project and pair each with a feasible range, so their prioritisation arguments carry numbers rather than adjectives. They can say, out loud and without embarrassment, which nodes in their own tree are identities and which are estimates with error bars. They check the residual before the headline, and notice when a rate is computed on a base of sixty-one before the board sets a target on it. And they re-root the tree when the business changes, treating that as a governance event rather than a spreadsheet edit.

12. What the two protagonists decided

Shaunak Bose re-rooted Rangat's tree at contribution margin, effective the October cycle, and kept revenue computed in parallel through December so the board could see both. He cancelled the engagement pod's renders-per-subscriber target, replacing it with a retention target that left the pod free to raise or lower render volume as the evidence warranted, and moved the quarter's largest engineering allocation to the distilled-model routing project on the strength of the 0.61 elasticity and the 22 percent feasible reduction — an expected +13.4 percent of contribution against +6.4 percent from the pricing change, which he approved but sequenced second. His stated reason was not that growth had been wrong but that the tree had been scoring a game the company had stopped playing.

Malini Rau went to the Pune offsite and declined to present an NRR tree. What she presented instead was an account ledger for the sixty-one accounts, with expansion and churn attached to named renewals and dates, and beneath it a genuine driver model on a single estimated node: claims-volume coverage. In FY26, all fourteen accounts above 40 percent coverage renewed and nine expanded, with mean expansion of 31 percent; of the seventeen below 15 percent coverage, three churned outright and six downgraded. She asked the board to set the target on coverage, which her teams and Farhan Qureshi's customer-success group in Hyderabad could move monthly, and to treat NRR as the reported consequence rather than the managed objective — conceding in the same breath that coverage was an estimated relationship, due for re-fitting every year, that might not hold.

1. Rangat's engagement pod did exactly what it was asked and made the company worse off. Where does the fault lie — with the target, with the tree, or with the person who chose the root in 2024 and never revisited it?

2. Malini is proposing that the board manage an estimated driver rather than an exact identity. What would have to be true for that to be the more rigorous choice, and what is the first sign it has gone wrong?

3. In your own product, name the node that no single team owns. Who currently resolves disputes about it, and on what cadence?

13. Going deeper

Turns the diagram into a management system and supplies the noise-floor discipline.

Node-level criteria; a tree of bad metrics reconciles perfectly and informs nothing.

The leaf test that would have caught Mandakini's approval rate before it carried a target.

Aarohan People Cloud: Forty-One Lakh Employees

A Bengaluru payroll platform pays more Indian employees every month than it ever has, and every team that owns a piece of that number has hit its target for six quarters running. Revenue has missed plan in four of them. The chief product officer has until Monday morning to explain the gap to a board that helped her build the diagram it came from.

1. Sunday night, Bellandur

At 11.10 p.m. on Sunday, 15 March 2026, Meera Sundaram was the only person on the fourth floor of Aarohan People Cloud's office on Outer Ring Road in Bellandur, Bengaluru, with the air-conditioning off and a whiteboard behind her that she had photographed twice and erased once. On the whiteboard, before she erased it, had been the company's metric tree: the diagram adopted at an offsite in Coorg in January 2024, printed on the wall of every floor, referenced by name in twenty-two job descriptions and in the objectives of every product and go-to-market team in India, Germany, Canada, Singapore and New Jersey.

It was 1.40 p.m. in Toronto. Priyanka Nair had been online for forty minutes and had sent Meera three files, the last of which was titled arpe_bridge_v9_DO_NOT_CIRCULATE.xlsx. Meera had opened it, closed it, and opened it again.

The numbers were not in dispute. In March 2026, Aarohan would run payroll for 41.6 lakh employees across 11,400 employer customers — the highest in the company's history, up from 18.2 lakh two years earlier. Net revenue for the financial year closing in sixteen days would come in at about ₹168 crore against a plan of ₹187 crore. The North Star had grown 129 per cent in two years. Revenue had grown 66 per cent. Nobody in the company had missed a target.

The board met at 10 a.m. on Monday at the Bellandur office, with two directors dialling in. Item four on the agenda was Meera's paper, "FY27 planning: the operating model". It contained three options. Sitting under the erased whiteboard, Meera had begun to suspect that the paper's defect was not which option it recommended but that all three options accepted the shape of the diagram she had just wiped off the wall.

2. How Aarohan got here

Aarohan People Cloud was founded in Bengaluru in 2018 by Vikram Chandrashekar, who had run enterprise sales at a mid-sized HR software firm, and Tanvi Bhagat, an engineer from Pune who had spent six years building reconciliation systems for a payments company. Their premise was narrow and correct: Indian payroll is not a spreadsheet problem but a compliance problem. Every monthly run has to reconcile EPFO contributions, ESIC, professional tax that differs by state, TDS under a regime that changes each Budget, and — since the platform began disbursing salaries directly — a bank file that must clear. Aarohan's first product did one thing that competitors did poorly: it closed the month.

By March 2026 the company employed 610 people, 480 of them in Bengaluru and Pune, and had raised ₹412 crore across three rounds. It was preparing a Series D.

The decision that shapes everything about the present situation was taken in November 2022, and at the time it was treated as the company's shrewdest commercial move. Aarohan signed a five-year embedded distribution agreement with Kalindi Payments, a merchant-acquiring and neobanking platform with about 1.9 lakh small-business customers. Kalindi would offer Aarohan payroll inside its own merchant dashboard, at a flat ₹399 per merchant per month bundled into the Kalindi subscription, with Kalindi retaining 30 per cent. Aarohan's cost of acquisition on that channel was effectively zero.

Two clauses in that agreement matter now. The first is an exclusivity clause: for as long as a merchant is served through Kalindi, Aarohan may not solicit that merchant directly, may not price to it directly, and may not upsell to it except through a Kalindi-approved campaign. The second is a data clause, drafted in the year the Digital Personal Data Protection Act was being digested by both legal teams: Kalindi is the data fiduciary for merchant and employee data on that channel, and passes Aarohan only a hashed merchant identifier, a state code, and a monthly count of employees processed. Aarohan therefore cannot see who those customers are, cannot measure how they behave, and cannot contact them.

In June 2024 the company made a second decision in the same spirit. To win a staffing and facilities-management client with 2.6 lakh workers on its books, it launched a contract-workforce module priced at ₹18 per employee per month, against a blended direct price then of about ₹52. Aditi Kulkarni's growth team modelled it as a volume play with a clear upgrade path. Sixteen such clients followed. Together the Kalindi channel and the contract-workforce module now account for 58 per cent of the employees Aarohan pays and 19 per cent of what it bills.

3. The industry

Indian payroll and HR software is not a winner-take-all market and shows no sign of becoming one. At the enterprise end, Darwinbox and the HR suites of the large Indian IT services firms compete on breadth; Zoho sells a full business suite at prices that make standalone payroll pricing difficult to hold; Keka and several well-funded challengers contest the mid-market; and a long tail of regional payroll bureaus and chartered accountants still process a large share of the country's salary runs by hand. Distribution increasingly runs through platforms rather than salespeople: Razorpay, Zoho and others embed payroll next to banking and invoicing, which is precisely the logic of the Kalindi deal.

Three forces bear directly on the product. First, the migration of salary disbursal to instant rails — the platform's bank files now settle through NPCI infrastructure in minutes rather than the next working day, which has made "salary credited on the first" a consumer expectation rather than an employer promise. Second, regulation: EPFO and ESIC filing formats, state professional tax schedules, and the annual TDS changes impose a fixed compliance load that must be borne whether a customer pays ₹18 or ₹62 per employee. Third, the DPDP Act, which has made every conversation about employee-level analytics a conversation with the legal team, and which underwrites Kalindi's refusal to share more than counts.

Aarohan's exposure outside India is small in employees and large in revenue concentration. A multi-country module, built in 2024 for the Gulf, supports UAE, Oman and Saudi payroll with Wage Protection System compliance. Its anchor customer is Qasr Facilities Management, a Dubai group with about 9,200 workers across three countries, worth ₹4.2 crore a year — 2.5 per cent of revenue from 0.2 per cent of the employees. Doug Whelan, in New Jersey, sells the same module to US companies with Indian subsidiaries; his six deals in FY26 averaged ₹68 lakh of annual contract value against an Indian direct average of ₹4.1 lakh.

4. The situation in detail

In January 2024, at a three-day offsite outside Madikeri, the leadership team chose a North Star. The candidates were net revenue, employer customers, and a measure of the work actually done for customers. Vikram argued for the third on the grounds that revenue is a lagging outcome and logos are a vanity count, and the room agreed on Monthly Paid Employees — MPE, the number of employees for whom Aarohan completed a payroll run in a calendar month. Priyanka Nair, then three months into the job, built the decomposition on the second morning. It is reproduced as Exhibit 1.

What made the diagram persuasive was that it multiplied out. MPE was employers on the platform, times employees per employer, times the share of those employees actually paid through Aarohan in the month. Each factor broke into levers, each lever had an owner and a cadence, and — in the version taken back to Bengaluru — a box in the bottom right converted MPE to revenue at ₹46 per employee per month. That box had no owner. The offsite minutes record it as "ARPE: held broadly constant; revisit annually."

For eighteen months the diagram worked in the way such diagrams are supposed to work. Teams stopped arguing about whose roadmap mattered. The weekly business review moved from forty slides to four. In October 2024, during the Diwali season, seasonal hiring at two large staffing clients pushed MPE up by 4.2 lakh in a single month, and the all-hands that week was, by common consent, the best in the company's history.

The first crack appeared in August 2025, when MPE grew 7 per cent in the quarter and net revenue grew 1.4 per cent. Arjun Pillai, the chief financial officer, raised it at the September review. The explanation offered — and accepted — was timing: the contract-workforce clients billed in arrears, the Kalindi channel recognised revenue a month late, and the quarter had one fewer working day at month-end. Meera remembers finding the explanation reasonable. She now believes it was three true statements assembled into a false one.

In November 2025 Arjun's revenue bridge showed something the tree could not show: ₹11 crore of the FY26 gap came from customers who had not churned. Their employee counts had fallen back after seasonal peaks, and because the contract-workforce contracts bill on actual monthly headcount with no floor, revenue fell with them. In the tree, these customers appeared in branch A as retained employers and in branch B as negative net employees added — a number Aditi Kulkarni's team was accountable for and could not influence, since it was driven by her customers' own hiring cycles.

In January 2026 Priyanka presented a driver model built to tell the company which levers actually moved retention. It is Exhibit 5. Its headline finding — that time-to-first-payroll was the strongest predictor of twelve-month retention — was welcomed, written into the FY27 draft plan as a ₹9 crore initiative, and has been repeated in three board updates since.

In February 2026, during Series D diligence, an analyst at the lead investor asked a question in a data-room comment thread that nobody at Aarohan had asked in that form: "Revenue per employee paid has declined 27% over two years. Is this mix or is this price?" Meera spent four weekends on the answer. The answer, as far as she can establish it, is in Exhibit 4, and it is not the answer she expected.

5. The people

Vikram Chandrashekar, 46, co-founder and chief executive, Bengaluru. Position: the North Star should not change during a fundraise. He argues, with some justice, that MPE is the only number in the company that a sales engineer in New Jersey, a support agent in Singapore and a platform engineer in Pune all understand the same way, and that it took two years to get there. Incentive: his own board narrative since 2024 has been built on MPE, and the Series D term sheet's ratchet references a growth rate that MPE comfortably clears and revenue does not. What he is not saying: he has privately told two directors that he would accept a slower FY27 if the company could show "revenue quality", and has not told the leadership team this.

Arjun Pillai, 49, chief financial officer, Bengaluru. Position: the tree should be rebuilt with net revenue at the top and the product teams should own revenue branches. Incentive: he is accountable to the board for the plan and has missed it four quarters in a row while every operating team reported green. What he is not saying: his own segment profitability model allocates platform and compliance cost per employee, which makes the contract-workforce module look worse than a per-customer allocation would, and he has not stress-tested the alternative.

Tanvi Bhagat, 44, co-founder and vice-president of engineering, Pune. Position: branch C is finished and she wants her 140 engineers redeployed. Run success is 99.94 per cent; the remaining failures are bank-side. Incentive: her strongest engineers are bored, and three have been approached by a Bengaluru infrastructure company at packages 30 per cent above Aarohan's Pune band. What she is not saying: she believes the Gulf multi-country work is a distraction that will consume two quarters of platform capacity for 2.5 per cent of revenue, and she has not said so in front of Doug Whelan.

Aditi Kulkarni, 35, director of product, growth, Bengaluru. Position: branch B is the wrong unit of accountability and always was; she can influence how many employees a customer onboards, not how many that customer employs. Incentive: her team's FY26 bonus is set against net employees added, which she will hit because of two large seasonal clients, and which she knows will reverse in April. What she is not saying: she proposed in May 2025 that the tree be split by segment, was told it would confuse the field, and has kept the deck.

Joachim Reuter, 38, head of design, Berlin. Position: the tree has no branch for the 41.6 lakh people whose salaries pass through the product, and a company that pays one in every hundred and fifty Indian formal-sector workers should not describe them as a unit of measure. Incentive: the employee app is his team's only owned surface and its measure is the one dashed box in Exhibit 1. What he is not saying: his own MAU figure is computed only on direct customers and therefore excludes 58 per cent of the base, which makes it flattering, and he raised this once, quietly, in a comment on a document.

Priyanka Nair, 33, staff data scientist, Toronto. Position: the tree is arithmetic, not causation, and should not be used to allocate engineering investment. Incentive: she built the tree at the offsite as a new joiner and it made her reputation in the company. What she is not saying: the driver model in Exhibit 5 has a collinearity problem she flagged in an appendix nobody read, and she has been asked twice to present the headline without the appendix.

Sharath Menon, 40, head of customer success, Singapore, covering South-East Asia and the Gulf. Position: activation is the highest-leverage branch and his numbers prove it. Incentive: he owns both activation and employer churn, and he owns the definition of activation. What he is not saying: the definition has been revised twice since 2024, most recently by his own team, and the revisions account for most of the improvement shown in Exhibit 6.

Doug Whelan, 52, senior vice-president of sales, New Jersey. Position: the company is undervaluing logos. Six Gulf and US deals produced ₹4.1 crore of annual contract value in FY26; 3,100 Kalindi merchants produced ₹1.5 crore. Incentive: his commission plan pays on annual contract value, not on employees. What he is not saying: two of his six deals, including Qasr, are contingent on roadmap commitments that Tanvi has not agreed to and that he has already described to the customers as committed.

Priyanka Nair, email to Meera Sundaram, Toronto, 13 March 2026

8. The options as Meera currently sees them

Option 1: keep MPE, re-cut the tree by segment. One North Star, four trees beneath it — enterprise, SMB, channel, contract — each with its own owners, its own ARPE and its own targets. This preserves the shared language Vikram values and makes mix visible for the first time. It also multiplies the number of owned measures from eight to about twenty-six, and Meera's own note against it reads: "we will have replaced one diagram nobody questions with four that nobody reads."

Option 2: move the North Star to net revenue retention. Arjun's position. It is the number the Series D investors are underwriting, it is auditable from the ledger, and it would make the contract-workforce seasonality visible in the metric itself rather than in a bridge. Against it: it is a lagging measure reported 45 days after month-end, it cannot be decomposed into anything an engineer in Pune can ship against, and on the Kalindi channel — 26 per cent of employees — Aarohan cannot compute it at customer level at all because it does not know who the customers are.

Option 3: replace ARPE's empty box with an owned branch. Keep MPE at the top but make revenue per employee a named factor with an owner, a cadence and a target, and make pricing, packaging and mix somebody's explicit job — probably Aditi's. This is the smallest change, it addresses the specific failure of the last two years, and it does not disturb anything before the Series D closes. Its weakness is that the person who would own it controls almost none of the things that move it: the Kalindi price is fixed by contract to 2027, the contract-workforce price was a board decision, and enterprise pricing sits with Doug.

Underneath the three options, on the last page of her paper, Meera has written a sentence she has not shown anyone. It is that every option assumes the tree's job is to describe the business, when for two years its actual job has been to divide it: to tell 610 people what they are accountable for and to settle arguments about capacity. A diagram can be a poor description of a company and still be the reason the company gets anything done — and the reverse is also true, which is the possibility she keeps circling back to. She does not know whether Monday's discussion is about measurement or about who reports to whom, and she is aware that if it is the second, the three options in her paper are all answers to the wrong question.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets at 10 a.m. IST on Monday, 16 March 2026, and the FY27 operating plan must be signed off by 31 March because compensation letters for the go-to-market organisation go out on 5 April and cannot be reissued. The Series D process is at the confirmatory diligence stage; the term sheet expires on 30 April and contains a milestone linked to a growth rate that MPE clears and net revenue does not. The Kalindi agreement auto-renews on 30 June 2026 unless either party gives ninety days' notice, which has now passed; its exclusivity and data clauses therefore bind until at least June 2027. The Qasr renewal, ₹4.2 crore, must be signed by 31 May, and the roadmap commitments Doug has described would take, on Tanvi's estimate, 22 developer-months across two quarters, against a December-quarter platform capacity of 31 developer-months of which 9 are already committed to DPDP data-residency work. Headcount is frozen at 610 until the round closes. Re-instrumenting the analytics pipeline to reconcile MPE with billed employees would take, on Priyanka's estimate, six weeks of work and a further eight weeks of forward data before any recomputed series could be trusted — which places the first reliable reconciled number after the FY27 plan is locked and after the Series D closes. Three of Tanvi's senior engineers have outstanding offers elsewhere. Aditi's team's bonus, already communicated, pays on net employees added.

10. Questions for discussion

1. Exhibit 1 shows eight owned measures and two unowned boxes. Which of the eight would you expect to improve without the business improving, and what in Exhibits 3, 6 and 7 tells you whether that has already happened?

2. Exhibit 2 gives two counts of the same employees that differ by 8.4 lakh, and Exhibit 7 gives two counts of the same merchants that differ by 9 per cent. For each, state what you can and cannot conclude, and say which decision on Monday's agenda actually depends on closing the gap.

3. Every segment in Exhibit 4 improved its price per employee while the blended figure fell 27 per cent. Explain the arithmetic to Vikram in three sentences, then say what it implies about branch A2 and branch B1 — and about the two decisions taken in 2022 and 2024 that produced the mix.

4. Exhibit 5 has already been written into a ₹9 crore FY27 initiative. Given Appendix B and the sample exclusions, what, if anything, should Meera do about that line in the plan before Monday, and what should she say to Priyanka about the appendix?

5. Aditi Kulkarni owns a branch she cannot influence, Tanvi Bhagat owns one that is finished, Sharath Menon owns both a measure and its definition, and Joachim Reuter owns a measure computed on 42 per cent of the base. Redesign the ownership, with cadences, without adding headcount. Which of the eight current owners loses the most, and how would you handle that conversation?

6. It is Monday morning. Meera has forty minutes, a frozen headcount, a channel contract that binds until June 2027, a plan that locks on 31 March, and a term sheet that references the growth rate of the number she may be about to demote. What does she put on the wall in place of the diagram she erased, what does she tell the board the company will stop measuring, and what does she say when a director asks the only question that matters to him — whether the last two years of green scorecards were wrong, or merely incomplete?

11. Sunday night, continued

At 12.50 a.m. Meera wrote to Priyanka: "Put Appendix B in. Slide 9 or slide 14, your choice." Then she deleted "your choice" and sent it. Toronto replied within a minute with a thumbs-up and nothing else, which Meera had learned to read as neither agreement nor forgiveness.

She took a photograph of the empty whiteboard, which she could not later explain to herself, and then drew on it a single box with the words employees paid inside, and stood looking at it for some time without drawing anything below. On the desk, her paper was open at the page with the three options; in the margin beside Option 3 she had written smallest true change, and beside that, later and in different ink, smallest change, anyway.

The cleaning staff came through at one. Meera took the lift down, and in the car park found that she was still thinking about a line from the Coorg minutes that she had reread that evening for the first time in two years: ARPE: held broadly constant; revisit annually. Nobody had revisited it. There had been no meeting at which the decision not to revisit it was taken, no owner to take it, and no cadence at which its absence would have been noticed. The board was in nine hours.

Kavach Insure: one number for four teams

Gurugram, October 2026. Policies sold are up 31 per cent. Revenue is up 9 per cent. Aparna Joshi has eleven days to tell the board which number the company will run on next year.

1. The Monday before the plan is due

On Monday, 19 October 2026 — the week after Dussehra, with Diwali eleven days away — Aparna Joshi arrived at Kavach Insure's office on Golf Course Road in Gurugram at seven in the morning, because it was the only hour when neither Bengaluru nor Toronto would message her. The annual operating plan was due to the board on 30 October. The chief executive, Harpreet Sandhu, had asked for one thing in it that had not been there the year before: a single North Star metric, and underneath it a written statement of which team owned which lever.

Aparna, VP Product for two and a half years, had the second half. What she did not have was agreement on the first. The number the company had used since 2023 — policies sold per month — had just delivered its best year and its worst. Policies were up 31 per cent year on year. Commission revenue was up 9 per cent. Both figures were correct, and the gap between them was the whole case.

2. Kavach Insure

Kavach Insure was founded in 2019 as an IRDAI-registered insurance broker selling policies online. A customer arriving from a search for "two-wheeler insurance renewal" could compare quotes from a dozen insurers, pay through UPI or a card via Razorpay, and have a policy document on WhatsApp in four minutes. The company competed with Policybazaar at the top of the market, with insurer-direct channels such as Acko and Go Digit, and with the bancassurance desks of every large bank; it distributed for ICICI Lombard, HDFC ERGO, Star Health and a dozen others, and earned a commission on each policy, plus a renewal commission where the product allowed one.

By FY26 the company intermediated about ₹1,180 crore of premium and booked ₹196 crore of commission revenue, with 640 employees. It had four product lines: retail motor, retail health, term life, and — added in 2023 — group health sold to companies, which is how a freight group in Dubai with 1,400 Indian employees came to be Kavach's third-largest single account. Two regulatory facts sat in the background of every planning conversation. The IRDAI's Bima Sugam marketplace was expected to compress distribution margins on simple products. And the DPDP Act's consent rules had, since 2025, made it materially harder to use data collected for a motor quote to sell a health policy eighteen months later.

The product organisation was distributed by design and by accident. Engineering sat in Bengaluru and Pune. Lena Wirth, the design lead, worked from Berlin and overlapped with India for half a day. Devesh Ramachandran, the senior data scientist who owned the lifetime-value model, was in Toronto, nine and a half hours behind. Priya Kandasamy ran customer success from Singapore, covering renewals for NRI customers across South-East Asia. Sunil Vaidya sold term life to the Indian diaspora from Edison, New Jersey, where a 45-year-old software engineer would buy ₹2 crore of Indian term cover without blinking.

3. The situation

The ₹49 flow had been Kavach's most successful product release. A returning two-wheeler owner could renew third-party cover in under ninety seconds with no document upload, paying a premium as low as ₹1,780 on which Kavach earned about ₹214. The growth team had followed it with cheap search and Meta traffic on motor-renewal intent, at an acquisition cost of ₹96 per policy. Motor's share of policies sold rose from 61 per cent to 72 per cent in fifteen months. Nobody had done anything wrong. Every incentive in the company pointed that way, because the number on the wall counted policies, and a motor policy counted exactly as much as a term policy that earned twenty-one times the commission.

Aparna had assembled the arithmetic in Exhibit 2. It showed that motor was 72 per cent of policies and 24 per cent of revenue; that health and term together were 28 per cent of policies and 65 per cent of revenue; and that group health, at twenty-six policies a month, was 11 per cent of revenue. Exhibit 3 added the part that worried her more: motor renewed at 41 per cent, health at 78 per cent, term persisted at 86 per cent and group renewed at 91 per cent. The company was buying, at growing volume, the customer who was least likely to come back.

The views from the other offices did not converge. Devesh had written from Toronto that his lifetime-value model put a motor customer at ₹430 and a health customer at ₹9,800, but had added a caveat in the same message: since the auto-debit mandate feature of late 2025, roughly 30,000 motor renewals a month were recorded as fresh policies, so both the policy count and the renewal rate were partly artefacts of instrumentation. Priya, in Singapore, pointed out that her renewal team's outbound calling was measured on policies retained, which made a ₹1,780 motor policy and a ₹46,000 health policy identical on her dashboard. Sunil, in New Jersey, wrote that he had a pipeline of NRI term cases worth ₹2.2 crore of annual commission and one product manager's attention for one day a fortnight, and that he could not get on any roadmap because his product line produced 8 per cent of the policy count.

4. The people

Aparna Joshi, VP Product, Gurugram, has to write the plan. She wants a structure in which each of her six product teams can state what it will move and be judged on it, and she is conscious that whatever number she proposes will shape hiring and bonuses for a year.

Rohit Bhandari, Chief Growth Officer, Gurugram, built the motor engine and defends it. His argument is not naive: volume builds the brand, the data asset and the cross-sell base, and in a market where Bima Sugam may commoditise comparison, Kavach's only defence is owning the customer relationship first. His team's variable pay is tied to policy volume, and he has said openly that he will not accept a revenue-rooted metric without a change to that scheme.

Nandita Sengupta, CFO, Mumbai, wants the North Star to be commission revenue, or better, contribution after acquisition cost. She has a board that asked, in July, why revenue per policy had fallen from ₹1,940 to ₹1,736 in a year, and she does not want to answer that question twice.

Devesh Ramachandran, senior data scientist, Toronto, is the only person who has looked hard at the data plumbing. He wants six weeks to fix the auto-debit classification before any new metric is adopted, and warns that a tree built on today's definitions will need restating in February.

5. Exhibits

Motor three-year value is below year-one revenue because the model discounts and because 59 per cent of motor customers do not renew. Motor renewal is understated by an unknown amount: since the auto-debit mandate shipped in November 2025, renewals through that path are classified as new policies. Devesh estimates the true motor renewal rate at 48 to 55 per cent and has requested six weeks to reclassify.

Read together, the two exhibits explain the year. Policies grew because the cheapest node in the tree — quote starts on motor intent — was also the easiest to buy. Revenue per policy fell 11 per cent because mix shifted toward the ₹576 product. And the ratio nobody had put on a dashboard, value divided by acquisition cost, was not obviously worse for motor; at 4.5 times it was respectable. Motor was not a bad business. It was a business that was being grown by a metric that could not tell the difference between ₹576 and ₹7.7 lakh.

6. The options

Option A: keep policies sold, add revenue as a guardrail. Nothing is re-plumbed, Rohit's incentive scheme is untouched, and the board sees continuity. A revenue floor is added: policies may grow only while revenue per policy stays above ₹1,700. The cost is that the mix node still has no owner, so the guardrail will be hit and then argued about, and the company will have spent a year discovering what Exhibit 3 already shows.

Option B: root the tree in commission revenue. Nandita's preference. The board conversation becomes simple and the mix problem disappears by construction, because mix is inside the metric. The costs are real: the growth and funnel teams now own a number they influence through three intervening steps, the metric rewards pushing the highest-commission product to whoever answers the phone — a genuine conduct risk in an IRDAI-regulated business — and Priya's renewal team, whose work shows up months later, becomes hard to plan around.

Option C: root the tree in active policies in force, with revenue as a parallel branch. The North Star becomes the count of customers currently covered, decomposed as retained policies plus new policies, with new policies decomposed by the existing funnel and retained policies owned by Priya. Revenue hangs beside it as policies-in-force × revenue per policy in force, with the mix node explicitly assigned — Aparna's proposal is to give it to the product-line owners jointly with insurer partnerships, and to set a mix target rather than leaving mix as a residue. The cost is complexity: two branches, a mix target that will be negotiated every quarter, and Devesh's warning that the retained-versus-new split cannot be measured correctly until the auto-debit classification is fixed.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Write out the arithmetic that reconciles +31 per cent policies with +9 per cent revenue. Which single node explains the gap, and who at Kavach owns it today?

2. Exhibit 4 shows motor at 4.5 times value over acquisition cost — healthy by most standards. Does that make the motor push a success, a mistake, or something else? What additional information would change your answer?

3. Rohit's incentive is tied to policy volume and he has said he will not accept a revenue root without a change to it. Is that an obstacle to the decision, or part of it?

4. Which option should Aparna put in the 30 October plan, and what exactly would she say to the board about Devesh's six weeks of data repair?

8. A note for the learner

This case is about the difference between a North Star metric and a metric tree. Kavach had the first and not the second. A North Star on its own is a slogan; it becomes an operating system only when it is written as an arithmetic decomposition in which every node has an owner, a cadence and a decision it informs. The diagnostic move is the one in question 1: commission revenue equals policies sold times revenue per policy, and revenue per policy is itself mix times rate per product. Once that is on paper, the year's mystery resolves in one line — the company owned every node on the left branch and no node on the right — and the choice between the three options becomes a choice about which nodes you are willing to make someone accountable for.

A well-reasoned answer will do three things. It will identify the unowned mix node as the cause rather than blaming the growth team, because the growth team optimised exactly what it was asked to. It will distinguish the identity — the arithmetic, which is not in dispute — from the estimates in Exhibit 4, which are contested and partly broken. And it will treat the instrumentation defect as a constraint on the plan rather than a reason to delay it.

One defensible path is Option C, with three specifics. First, adopt active policies in force as the North Star, because it is a measure of customers actually served, it rises for both new business and retention, and it cannot be inflated by the auto-debit misclassification that corrupts the policy count. Second, publish revenue per policy in force as a named, owned node with a floor — not a guardrail buried in a footnote — and assign mix to the product-line owners with a quarterly target, so that the decision to grow motor becomes an explicit choice rather than a by-product of media buying. Third, take Devesh's six weeks, but take them in parallel: adopt the tree on 30 October, state in the plan that the new-versus-retained split will be restated in the February review, and show the board the restatement when it comes. The board will forgive a labelled correction; it will not forgive discovering the same gap a second year running.

Option B is not wrong, and a reader who argues for it should be pushed on two things: what happens to advisor conduct when the company's single number rewards selling the highest-commission product, and how the funnel teams in Bengaluru will form a testable quarterly claim about a number three steps away from their work. Option A is the one to argue against hardest, because it looks like prudence and is in fact a decision to spend another year without an owner on the node that matters.
